## Project overview

This analysis explores two questions using 500 Facebook posts from a cosmetics brand: (1) how does engagement vary with posting time and content type, and (2) how does paid promotion relate to engagement? Engagement is measured by **Total Interactions** (likes + comments + shares). These observational data cannot establish causal effects or advertising return on investment.

## Setup and data preparation

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
set.seed(320)
# Render from the repository root, e.g. rmarkdown::render("analysis/facebook_engagement.Rmd")
posts <- readr::read_delim("data/facebook_posts.csv", delim = ";", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  transmute(
    type = factor(Type),
    month = factor(`Post Month`, levels = 1:12, labels = month.abb),
    weekday = factor(`Post Weekday`, levels = 1:7,
                     labels = c("Sun", "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat")),
    hour = as.integer(`Post Hour`),
    paid = factor(Paid, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Organic", "Paid")),
    reach = as.numeric(`Lifetime Post Total Reach`),
    interactions = as.numeric(`Total Interactions`)
  )
knitr::kable(posts %>% count(type), caption = "Posts by content type")
summary(posts$interactions)
```

The data contain 500 posts; some promotion values are missing. Model-specific missing observations are omitted explicitly below. Weekday codes use Sunday = 1, Saturday = 7. Hour is recorded in 24-hour time.

## Exploratory analysis

```{r engagement-by-type, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
ggplot(posts, aes(type, interactions)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.25) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, quantile(posts$interactions, .95, na.rm = TRUE))) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of interactions by post type", x = "Post type", y = "Total interactions (view limited to 95th percentile)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The next heatmap is descriptive, not a prediction. To reduce the visual impact of extreme posts, it excludes observations above the 95th percentile; this changes the population being summarized. Sparse day-hour-type combinations can produce unstable averages.

```{r heatmap, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
heatmap_data <- posts %>%
  filter(interactions <= quantile(interactions, .95, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(type, weekday, hour) %>%
  summarise(mean_interactions = mean(interactions), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(hour, weekday, fill = mean_interactions)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") + facet_wrap(~type) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Average interactions by posting time and type", subtitle = "Top 5% of posts excluded; cells may contain few posts", x = "Hour (24-hour clock)", y = "Day", fill = "Mean interactions") + theme_minimal()
```

## Comparing timing models

We compare eight linear regression specifications. Unlike the original classroom draft, the error measures below use a held-out test set instead of the same observations used to fit the models. The test set is only a basic check; a larger independent dataset would provide stronger evidence of generalization. The model with hour-by-day interaction can be unstable when combinations are rare, so hour is treated as numeric in these models.

```{r model-comparison}
model_data <- posts %>% drop_na(interactions, hour, weekday, month)
train_ids <- sample(seq_len(nrow(model_data)), size = floor(.8 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[train_ids, ]
test <- model_data[-train_ids, ]
formulas <- list(
  "Hour" = interactions ~ hour,
  "Weekday" = interactions ~ weekday,
  "Month" = interactions ~ month,
  "Hour + weekday" = interactions ~ hour + weekday,
  "Hour + month" = interactions ~ hour + month,
  "Weekday + month" = interactions ~ weekday + month,
  "All timing variables" = interactions ~ hour + weekday + month,
  "Hour × weekday + month" = interactions ~ hour * weekday + month
)
metrics <- purrr::imap_dfr(formulas, function(formula, name) {
  fit <- lm(formula, data = train)
  prediction <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
  tibble(model = name, MAE = mean(abs(test$interactions - prediction)),
         MSE = mean((test$interactions - prediction)^2),
         RMSE = sqrt(MSE))
}) %>% arrange(MAE)
knitr::kable(metrics, digits = 2, caption = "Holdout prediction errors (lower is better)")
```

MAE is the average absolute prediction error; MSE is the average squared error. MSE penalizes unusually large errors more strongly. Lower training error alone does not prove a more complex model predicts better.

## Probability of high engagement

High engagement is defined as total interactions at or above the **training-set** 75th percentile. This definition avoids choosing the threshold using test outcomes. The model estimates associations, not guaranteed optimal posting times.

```{r logistic-model, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
cutoff <- quantile(train$interactions, .75)
train <- train %>% mutate(high_engagement = as.integer(interactions >= cutoff))
test <- test %>% mutate(high_engagement = as.integer(interactions >= cutoff))
logit <- glm(high_engagement ~ hour + weekday + month, data = train, family = binomial())
prob <- predict(logit, newdata = test, type = "response")
knitr::kable(tibble(
  threshold = cutoff,
  test_brier_score = mean((test$high_engagement - prob)^2),
  baseline_brier_score = mean((test$high_engagement - mean(train$high_engagement))^2)
), digits = 3, caption = "Test-set Brier score (lower is better)")
new_times <- expand_grid(hour = sort(unique(posts$hour)),
                         weekday = levels(posts$weekday),
                         month = levels(posts$month)) %>%
  mutate(weekday = factor(weekday, levels = levels(posts$weekday)),
         month = factor(month, levels = levels(posts$month)),
         probability = predict(logit, newdata = ., type = "response"))
ggplot(new_times, aes(hour, weekday, fill = probability)) +
  geom_tile() + facet_wrap(~month, ncol = 4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Modeled probability of high engagement", x = "Hour", y = "Day", fill = "Probability") + theme_minimal()
```

## Paid promotion and post type

```{r paid-comparison, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
paid_data <- posts %>% drop_na(paid, interactions)
paid_summary <- paid_data %>% group_by(type, paid) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean_interactions = mean(interactions),
            median_interactions = median(interactions), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(paid_summary, digits = 1, caption = "Observed engagement by content and promotion")
ggplot(paid_summary, aes(type, mean_interactions, fill = paid)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Average interactions: paid vs. organic", x = "Content type", y = "Mean interactions", fill = "Promotion") + theme_minimal()
```

```{r paid-regression}
paid_fit <- lm(interactions ~ paid * type + hour, data = paid_data)
knitr::kable(broom::tidy(paid_fit), digits = 3,
             caption = "Exploratory regression with promotion-by-type interactions")
```

The coefficients describe adjusted associations under this specification. A non-significant coefficient is not proof of no effect, and individual interaction coefficients depend on the reference category. The model does not account for all potential confounders.

## Reach and interactions

Reach and interactions are both post-performance outcomes. Their association **cannot** identify diminishing returns to advertising spend because the dataset contains no spending amounts. The quadratic fit below is descriptive.

```{r reach-model, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
reach_data <- posts %>% drop_na(reach, interactions)
reach_fit <- lm(interactions ~ reach + I(reach^2), data = reach_data)
knitr::kable(broom::tidy(reach_fit), digits = 5)
ggplot(reach_data, aes(reach, interactions)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Association between post reach and interactions",
       subtitle = "Quadratic trend; not an estimate of advertising ROI",
       x = "Lifetime reach", y = "Total interactions") + theme_minimal()
```

## Conclusions and limitations

- Engagement varies substantially across content types and individual posts; descriptive averages for sparse posting-time cells should be interpreted cautiously.
- Compare the holdout errors and logistic model's Brier score before claiming that posting-time variables predict engagement reliably.
- Paid and organic posts differ in observed engagement, but the dataset does not support causal claims about paid promotion.
- Without promotion costs, it is not possible to estimate return on ad spend or an optimal advertising budget.
- Results come from a single brand and historical posts; generalization to other brands, platforms, or years is uncertain.

**Possible next steps:** repeated cross-validation, uncertainty intervals for subgroup averages, richer features, and access to ad spend and targeting data.

## Data source

Moro, Rita, and Vala (2016), *Facebook metrics* dataset, UCI Machine Learning Repository. See the repository README for source and attribution.
